title: Transient capacity bridge & GPU rehab playbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft runbook for short-term capacity bridging and GPU cartridge / node rehabilitation during infra incidents. Focus: get customer-facing capacity back quickly while keeping safety for model state (KV caches), avoiding corrupted GPUs, and preserving rollout invariants.

Scope (when to use):
- Thermal trips that take a rack / zone below target capacity and we need immediate short-term capacity injection (minutes-hours).
- Faulty GPU module or dGPU that repeatedly triggers ECC/soft errors and needs cartridge swap or node replacement.
- Smart cordon/drain when eviction would cause unacceptable tail latency for long-lived sessions (chat, streaming).
- NOT for planned maintenance (use maintenance playbook) or full datacenter evacuation.

Quick triage (first 10 minutes):
- Check alert details: source (prometheus/sentry/hardware-alert), scope (rack/node/GPU), and impact (p50/p95 latency, error spikes).
- Run `sre/triage/check-capacity` script (equivalent: kubectl get pods -n inference -o wide, node-exporter for thermal, gpu-health for ECC).
- Post to slack #sre-oncall: short summary + incident label + expected MTR (e.g., "thermal trip, zone B, -20% capacity, estimating 30-90m") and tag eng-platform and serving-runtime.
- If customer-facing slowdown: flip routing policy to bridge-mode (see section: routing fast fallback).

Safety prerequisites (do before physical actions):
- Ensure no active model rollouts are mid-canary for affected model versions. If a rollout is in-progress, coordinate with model-ops and halt until safe.
- Snapshot any long-lived KV caches if supported. Note: snapshots can be expensive — only when chat sessions >1k impacted.
- Record current allocation `infra-capacity/snapshot-<ts>` (automated script) to allow rollback.

Immediate containment steps (software-first):
1) Quick isolate: `kubectl cordon <node>` to stop new scheduling. Leave running user pods if they are low-priority and can be drained gracefully.
2) Graceful drain policy: use `kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120` only for nodes that show persistent GPU failure. If pods have in-memory state, coordinate with session-migration hooks (serving-runtime has migration flag).
3) Adjust autoscaler: temporarily allow surge if autoscaler blocked by nodeGroup limits. Patch cluster-autoscaler scale-up to +2 capacity for the affected zone (tag: emergency-bridge).
4) Apply incremental routing: update `router-config` to shift 30-50% of traffic away from affected hardware to healthy pools (fast-fallback policy). Monitor for increased latencies elsewhere.

Physical GPU cartridge replacement (if hardware team on-site / remote hands):
- Preconditions: node cordoned and drained of critical workloads, power fencing scheduled, ESD precautions in place.
- Tools: GPU extraction tool, spare cartridge from hot-swap rack (labelled), replacement thermal pads, screw kit, firmware USB image (if needed).
- Steps (high-level):
  a) Verify node offline state in console and `ipmi` shows stable state.
  b) Power off host via BMC. Wait for safe shutdown confirmation.
  c) Remove faulty cartridge per vendor guide (note: different vendors have different latch orientation). Place faulty unit into antistatic bag and label with failure id.
  d) Install replacement cartridge, verify seating, reattach cooling.
  e) Power on and watch BMC logs for GPU POST. If POST passes, run `gpu-health-check --quick` which runs ECC self-test and thermal probe checks.
  f) If health-check passes, mark node `unschedulable=false` and allow autoscaler to re-evaluate. If not, re-cordon and escalate to hardware vendor.

Hot-swap caveats:
- Avoid hot-swap while heavy KV writes are happening — can corrupt cache indices. Prefer swapping nodes that are already drained.
- If replacement shows intermittent ECC reappearance within 30 minutes, quarantine spare pool and open hardware ticket (JIRA-1193 or new ticket).

Cluster recovery after thermal trip / IO surge:
- Step 1: throttle new session creation for 10–20 minutes using rate limiter. This prevents thundering herd when nodes come back.
- Step 2: bring up backfill nodes in a staged manner (10% increments) to monitor tail latencies.
- Step 3: run health gating: `kpi-checks` for p50/p95 latency, error rate, token throughput. Only advance stages if all gates pass.
- Step 4: roll traffic back from bridge pools to primary pools slowly (10% every 5 minutes) and monitor for regressions.

Emergency capacity add (short-term backfill):
- Where possible use pre-warmed spare instances (hot-pool) first. Hot-pool should be part of Dedicated capacity config.
- If hot-pool is exhausted, spin new nodes in compatible instance type with quantized model variant (lower memory but same API surface) to accept burst traffic. Document expected quality delta to product/CS.
- Coordinate billing/finance: tag emerg-capacity-<incident-ts> to track overruns.

Validation and testing (post-fix):
- Run a synthetic traffic profile that mimics customer scenarios (chat streaming, embeddings batch) to validate correctness and perf.
- Validate model outputs against golden prompt set for high-risk customers (tie to Redwood Optimize checks).
- Confirm logs, traces, and token-cost accounting resumed normal state.

Communication checklist:
- T+0: Slack summary in #sre-oncall and #incidents: short impact + owner + ETA for next update.
- T+15: post triage findings and temporary mitigations.
- T+60 or on resolution: update incident channel with root cause hypothesis and next steps.
- Postmortem: assign owner and draft within 72 hours (link to incident doc and RCA).

Rollback and unsafe states:
- If replacement worsens metrics (increased p99 error or CPU steal), immediately revert routing to last-known-good using `router rollback <id>`.
- If replacement triggers rollback twice, escalate to infra leadership and prepare for cluster-wide QA freeze.

Post-incident notes (for this draft):
- TODO: add step-by-step vendor-specific extraction pictures and part numbers for our current hardware mix (A100-80G, H100 etc.).
- TODO: inline commands for `gpu-health-check` and `kpi-checks` scripts — currently referenced but not included.
- Unresolved: automated snapshot trigger thresholds for KV caches — how many sessions warrant snapshot? (Maya to propose).

Recent test run notes (simulated):
- 2026-02-14 thermal-sim run: hot-pool injection + staged routing prevented p95 regressions in 6/7 simulated runs. Root cause was radiator fan firmware causing thermal climb.
- Action: schedule firmware roll for affected chassis group during next maintenance window.

Contacts and escalation ladder:
- Oncall SRE: primary #sre-oncall, backup is Liam O'Connor.
- Hardware vendor (on-call): Diego Alvarez -> vendor-admin@hw-vendor.example.com.
- Serving runtime lead: Maya Chen.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep this doc short; split vendor-specific checklists to subdocs under `hardware-guides/` to avoid bloat.
- Remember to tag any rapid-capacity spend for finance reconciliation.

End of draft — leave feedback inline and add concrete commands to replace placeholders.
